title: Success-Conditioning as Policy Improvement: The Optimization Problem Solved by Imitating Success
claim: The standard divergence penalty forbids concentrating on one action, while our alternative constraint permits concentration but penalizes mass shifted toward rare actions.
layout: 2 vertically stacked panels, top-to-bottom, red versus blue contour maps on a simplex
description: Two vertically stacked contour plots on the probability simplex for a three-action problem. Both panels have π(a1) on the x-axis and π(a2) on the y-axis. A diagonal black line marks the simplex boundary, and the area above it is shaded gray. A black dot marks the initial policy π0 near (0.49, 0.49). The top panel is titled 'KL Trust Region (TRPO/PPO): Forgetting is expensive'. It shows red contours labeled 0.05, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.50. They close off before the a2 corner, which has a black X, and the label reads 'Concentration prohibited'. The bottom panel is titled 'χ² Trust Region (Success Conditioning): Exploring is expensive'. It shows blue contours labeled 0.1, 0.4, 1.0 and 2.0. They stretch toward the a2 corner, which has a gold star, and the label reads 'Concentration permitted'. The eye goes first to the red versus blue contrast and the corner markers.
caption: Trust region geometry for a three-action problem with $\pi_0 = (0.49, 0.49, 0.02)$. The simplex constraint restricts policies to the region below the diagonal. Top: KL prohibits concentration. Bottom: $\chi^2$ permits concentration but penalizes shifting mass toward actions that are rare under $\pi_0$.
abstract: A widely used technique for improving policies is success conditioning, in which one collects trajectories, identifies those that achieve a desired outcome, and updates the policy to imitate the actions taken along successful trajectories. This principle appears under many names -- rejection sampling with SFT, goal-conditioned RL, Decision Transformers -- yet what optimization problem it solves, if any, has remained unclear. We prove that success conditioning exactly solves a trust-region optimization problem, maximizing policy improvement subject to a $Ï^2$ divergence constraint whose radius is determined automatically by the data. This yields an identity: relative policy improvement, the magnitude of policy change, and a quantity we call action-influence -- measuring how random variation in action choices affects success rates -- are exactly equal at every state. Success conditioning thus emerges as a conservative improvement operator. Exact success conditioning cannot degrade performance or induce dangerous distribution shift, but when it fails, it does so observably, by hardly changing the policy at all. We apply our theory to the common practice of return thresholding, showing this can amplify improvement, but at the cost of potential misalignment with the true objective.
